KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Record high temperatures are occurring this afternoon in the
warm sector of a low pressure system moving through the central
Great Lakes. Warm air advection with 850 mb temps of 18-19 C,
sunny skies, and gusty SW winds have led to surface temperatures
in the mid 80s, with even isolated upper 80s in NW Ohio! This
will set up a very warm and breezy evening.

The surface low will move into the eastern Great Lakes tonight,
dragging a cold front to the vicinity of Lake Erie this evening.
The front will become quasi-stationary near the south shore of
the lake for several hours tonight as a secondary mid-level
shortwave emanating out of a cut off low over the Four Corners
region crosses the southern and central Great Lakes. This will
result in a weak surface wave riding along the front tonight.
The combination of this surface wave and 130+ knot H3 and 60-70
knot H5 jets associated with the mid/upper wave crossing the 
Great Lakes will enhance large scale forcing to generate showers
and thunderstorms along the front late tonight and early 
Wednesday morning as it sags southward. The 12Z suite of HREF
CAMS have become more aggressive with a cluster of convective
showers and even some thunder developing in SE Lower Michigan
and NW Ohio overnight then progressing across Lake Erie and the
adjacent lakeshore counties of northern and NE Ohio in the
08-11Z timeframe. This is not shown nearly as much by the RRFS,
but the aforementioned forcing tied to the surface and mid/upper
waves traversing the sagging boundary support some convection,
especially with lingering warmth overnight from today's record
highs (lows in the mid 60s). The key will be Lake Erie. HREF
and RRFS instability parameters suggest little to no surface or
MUCAPE overnight, but the warm Lake Erie waters averaging 18C
will likely generate some over-lake instability. This could help
the convective cluster to become more organized over the lake as
it moves east, and if so, the presence of 50 knots of westerly
0-6 Km bulk shear could cause strong to sub severe winds near
the lakeshore. This probability is low overall and conditional
on if the cluster can get a boost over the lake, but if any
convective winds occur, the most likely area would be from
roughly just east of Toledo through the Islands to Lake, 
Geauga, and Ashtabula Counties where the weak instability over 
and near the lake will aid in momentum transfer to the surface.

Additional showers and pockets of embedded thunder with heavier
downpours will continue Wednesday as the cold frontal boundary 
continues pushing southward, but widespread cloud cover and the 
best jet support progressing east of the region will prevent 
anything organized, with mainly low-impact rain expected. The
best potential for heavier rain and thunder will be along and
south of the US-30 corridor in the afternoon. Overall QPF
Wednesday will average a few hundredths to up to 0.20 in most
areas, but some 0.25 to 0.50 inch amounts could occur along and
south of US 30 if any isolated convective showers/thunder can
redevelop in the afternoon. Any rain will trend farther south as
the day wears on, with slow drying from north to south expected.
All areas will be dry by Wednesday night as Canadian high
pressure building into the Upper Great Lakes pushes the front
into the Ohio River Valley.  

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The break in the weather will be brief as the Canadian high
across the Great Lakes already retreats Thursday afternoon to
allow the frontal boundary to lift back north as a warm front
Thursday evening and night. This is in response to the old Four
Corners cut off low phasing with an amplifying mid/upper trough
through the northern Plains/Upper Midwest. The result will be a
deep, negatively tilted trough digging through the Great Lakes
and eastern U.S. Friday and Saturday. In response to this
dynamic trough, strong surface cyclogenesis will take place over
the southern Great Lakes Friday morning, with the deepening low
lifting across upstate NY during the day. 

In terms of impacts, rain will lift back into the region late
Thursday afternoon and evening as warm air advection and
isentropic ascent generate a rain shield along and north of the
lifting warm front. There will likely be a lull in the warm
sector Thursday night with gusty SW winds developing (gusting up
to 30 knots) beneath a 50+ knot low-level jet, but showers will
fill back in ahead of the strong cold front that will cross the
region Friday morning. Will need to watch for a low-topped 
squall line along the front if at least weak instability can be 
realized since the strong wind fields could produce damaging 
winds. Nevertheless, strong cold air advection in the wake of 
the front, the tight pressure gradient, and strong post-frontal 
pressure rises will lead to strong winds Friday morning into
